High- throughput RNA sequencing and genetic structure studies of turnip mosaic virus infecting black and yellow mustard revealing emergence of world- B3 pathotype in
India
Pankhuri Singhal1 | Virendra Kumar Baranwal1 | Malyaj R. Prajapati2 |
Jitender Singh2
1Division of Plant Pathology, ICAR- Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi, India
2College of Biotechnology, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel University of Agriculture and Technology, Meerut, India
Abstract

The RNA viruses are marked by high genetic diversity, which allows them to quickly adapt to new and resistant hosts. The pathogenic turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) infects Brassicaceae plant species all over the world.
Aim: To study the evolution and host expansion of a TuMV for the first time in India using molecular population genetic framework.
Correspondence
Virendra Kumar Baranwal, Division of Plant Pathology, ICAR- Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi 110012, India. Email: vbaranwal2001@yahoo.com

Materials and Results: Here, we decipher the complete genome sequences of two TuMV world- B3 strains infecting yellow and black mustard in India through high- throughput RNA sequencing subjecting ribosomal RNA depleted mRNA isolated from leaves exhibiting puckering and mosaic symptoms with 100% incidence and high severity in the experimental field. The viral genomes of the two isolates were 9817 and 9829 nucleotides long. They featured two open reading frames (ORFs), one of which encoded a polyprotein comprised of 3164 amino acids and the other of which encoded a PIPO protein of 62 amino acids.

Conclusions: The two TuMV strains from New Delhi region shared identity with the world- B pathotype and subpathotype world B3 showcasing its emergence first time in South Asia. In contrast, other isolates reported previously from South Asia were all Asian- BR pathotypes.

Significance and Impact of the Study: According to our knowledge, this is the first instance of TuMV association with black mustard naturally. Their geographical prevalence justifies a lower degree of genetic differentiation and higher rate of gene flow calculated between the world- B and Asian- BR pathotypes. This study provides insights on population structuring, expansions and evolution, level of genetic hetero- geneity and variability of worldwide prevalent isolates of TuMV which will further aid in understanding virus epidemiology and help prevent losses.

INTRODUCTION

Oilseed mustard (family Brassicaceae) is the third primary source of edible oil after soybean and palm oil in the world (Rimmer, 1995), and it has several plant species in the genera. Besides seeds being of importance, the leaves of young plants are also used as a vegetable. Mustard is the 2nd most important oilseed crop in India after soybean. India is 3rd largest producer of mustard after Canada and China. The basic types are yellow mustard (Brassica rapa subsp trilocularis), considered of Mediterranean origin; brown; Indian mustard (Brassica juncea), considered of Himalayan origin; and black mustard (B. nigra), consid- ered of Asia Minor- Iran.

The mosaic disease of crucifers dates back to as old as the early 1900s when it was noticed in turnip (Gardner & Kendrik, 1921). The main symptoms associated with the mosaic disease include mosaic with leaf distortion and necrosis, especially on lower leaves, dwarfing of plants and senescence (Tompkins, 1938). Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) is the main virus thought to be the causative agent of mosaic disease. The TuMV is a member of the Potyvirus genus with a vast host range infecting approximately 156 genera of 43 families representing several arable, vegeta- ble and ornamental crops. But its main hosts are found in the family Brassicaceae (Tomimura et al., 2003; Walsh & Jenner, 2002). In a review of viral diseases in 28 nations and regions, TuMV was placed second only to the cucum- ber mosaic virus as the most significant virus affecting vegetables as well as oilseeds (Tomlinson, 1987). TuMV infection is particularly detrimental to brassicid crops in portions of Europe, Asia and North America, resulting in production losses of up to 70% (Li et al., 2019). The yield re- ductions in TuMV plants showing severe virus symptoms were estimated to be 70% to 79% (Hardwick et al., 1994). In China, the mosaic- inducing viruses of rape seed caused 30% losses of the crop which estimated 50%– 80% yield loss (Shen, 1965). Losses caused by turnip mosaic in Germany
may vary from 1% to 90% (Pape, 1935).

The TuMV is a flexuous filamentous particle of 700– 750 × 12 nm made up of a single copy of single- stranded, positive- sense RNA (+ssRNA) of nearly 9830 nt, which is infectious and acts both as genomic and viral messenger RNA (mRNA). The result of genomic RNA translation is a single large polyprotein of 3164 amino acids, which is fur- ther subjected to the action of three self- encoded protein- ases: Pl, HC- Pro and NIa- Pro resulting in 10 functional proteins (King & Adams, 2012). Moreover, P3N- PIPO, a lately identified protein, is produced via a + 1/+2 ribo- somal frameshift inside the P3 ORF and may function as a movement protein (Chung et al., 2008).
The TuMV is transmitted by polyphagous aphids, and infected plant materials such as seed only in radish

(Berthelot et al., 2019; Tomlinson & Walker, 1973). The TuMV's nucleotide evolutionary rate is roughly 10−3 substitutions per site per year on average (Nguyen et al., 2013). The world- B isolates have been reported from brassicas from all the continents, and these are further subdivided into three subgroups. The three sub- groups of world- B are world- B1 consisting of isolates from Russia and Poland; world- B2 representing isolates from Ukraine, Czech Republic, Denmark and Turkey; world- B3 comprising isolates from Europe, East Asia and South- East Asia, B3 containing both B and B(R) pathotypes (Kawakubo et al., 2021). The Asian- BR group might have emerged in either Turkey or Iran and subse- quently spread to the rest of the world, including South Asia, where radish is grown. The evolution of plant virus populations is driven by founder effects, selection and re- combination indicated by the genetic structure studies of viral populations genomes. The evolution of TuMV, like that of other potyviruses, is marked by frequent recombi- nation (Yasaka et al., 2015).

Knowledge of viral genetic diversity has been imper- ative for the efficient management of diseases caused by them (Pallás et al., 2018; Rubio et al., 2020). The applica- tion of high- throughput sequencing (HTS) such as DNA/ RNA- seq, virion- associated nucleic acids (VANA) purified from virus- like particles, double- stranded RNAs (dsRNA) and virus- derived small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) has largely contributed to understand the comprehensive- ness of plant virome and virus variability as it provides a generic approach to identify or characterize the viral agent(s) present in a plant without previous knowledge of the virus structure or sequence (Hadidi et al., 2016; Prajapati et al., 2022; Roossinck, 2017).

In India, the incidence of the mosaic disease has been reported from various regions from radish and brown mustard (Ahlawat, 1984; Haq et al., 1994; Parmar et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2015). But these reports were just based on mere incidence based on symptoms, biological studies or PCR amplification of partial coat protein region of the TuMV. No further studies on the complete genome identification and its evolution as well as variability have been conducted so far. Thus, on observing virus symp- toms (mosaic and puckering) in mustard fields in Indian agricultural research institute (IARI), New Delhi, symp- tomatic samples were collected and pooled samples were subjected to virome analysis to determine the causative factor. In this work, the entire genome sequences of two TuMV strains obtained from black and yellow mustard were determined. Together with 34 additional previously published, representative TuMV isolates obtained from various hosts throughout the world, we evaluated the phy- logenetic relations, recombination pattern and genetic di- versity of these isolates.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Collection of virus infected samples and electron microscopic studies

The symptoms of viral disease were observed in the ex- perimental field of mustard during January 2021 and 2022 at the IARI, New Delhi (Figure 1a). The leaf samples from genotypes of black, yellow and brown mustard exhibiting suspected symptoms of viral diseases such as predomi- nantly puckering, along with mosaic, and stunting were collected and stored at −80°C till further analysis. The symptomatic leaf samples collected from the field were ex- amined under an electron microscope (EM) following the leaf dip method using 2% aqueous uranyl acetate (UA).
High- throughput RNAseq, sequence processing and assembly

The symptomatic leaf samples from each variety were subjected to total RNA extraction individually using Qiagen RNeasy plant mini kit in accordance with the user instructions manual. The total RNA's quality and quan- tity were assessed using Qubit™ fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and tapestation. The ribosomal RNA was subtracted from the total RNA using the Ribo- Zero rRNA Removal Kit (Illumina). RNA was quantified by the nanodrop spectrophotometer. Libraries were prepared using truseq- stranded- total RNA library preparation kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Bioanalyzer (Agilent) and tapestation were used to verify the quality of the sequence library acquired. The sequenc- ing was conducted using Illumina Novaseq 6000.

After sequencing, quality control of fastq paired end reads was performed using FastP v.0.20.0 to remove adapt- ers, poly- N sequences (≥15%) and filter off low- quality reads. The RNAseq for samples was assembled using
Sequence validation through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and sequencing

The assembled TuMV genomes were validated using two- step reverse transcriptase- polymerase chain reac- tion (RT- PCR) followed by sequencing of the amplified products. The Illumina assembled virus sequences were aligned together using ClustalW multiple sequence align- ment program with default parameters as implemented in BioEdit v.7.2.3. A consensus sequence obtained was used to design PCR primers for P3 gene (Forward— 5′GGAA CAGAGTGGGAGGAC 3′ and Reverse— 3′TTGATGA AC TACTACCTTTTC 5′) and Coat protein (CP) gene (Forward— 5′GCAGGTGAAACGCTTGATGCAGG 3′ and Reverse— 3′TAACCCCTTAACGCCAAGTAA 5′) manu- ally with amplicon size of 1065 and 864 bp, respectively. The first strand of c- DNA was synthesized using FIREScript® RT cDNA synthesis kit as per the manufacturer's protocol with a slight modification. The cDNA was further ampli- fied using standard PCR consisting of initial denaturation step at 94°C for 4 min, 35 cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 45 s, annealing at 44°C for P3/60°C for CP for 1 min and extension at 72°C for 1 min, followed by final primer extension at 72°C for 10 min. The PCR mixture consisted of 1000 ng of cDNA template, 12.5 μl DreamTaq™ green PCR master mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific®) and 1 μl each of forward and reverse primer in a total volume of 25 μl. PCR- amplified products were electrophoretically separated on 1% agarose gel containing 0.01% ethidium bromide, prepared in 1X TAE (Tris– Acetic acid– EDTA). After electrophoresis, the amplification products were vis-
ualized in a gel documentation system (BIO- RAD). After

The puri- fied PCR products were cloned into pGEM- T easy vector (Promega) followed by sequencing at eurofins genomics India, Bengaluru, in both directions using SP6 and T7 uni- versal primer pair and sequence analysis was performed. Consensus sequences were verified using BLASTN 2.9.0+ and comparisons were made with the complete TuMV se- quences assembled from Illumina reads.
The incidence of TuMV infection in mustard genotypes was calculated based on the number of positive samples against the total number of samples tested represented as percentage.
Sequence, phylogenetic and diversity analyses

Multiple sequence alignments were performed using ClustalW (Thompson et al., 1994) implemented in MEGA version XI (Tamura et al., 2021). The aligned sequences of nucleotides and amino acids were used to locate ORFs along with nine putative cleavage sites and conserved motifs in the sequences of two TuMV strains (Adams et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2016) which were further vali- dated through NCBI ORF finder (https://www.ncbi.nlm. nih.gov/orffi nder/) and Expasy (https://web.expasy.org/ trans late/). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using the maximum- likelihood with 1000 bootstrapping for the evaluation of branch validity. The codons of inter- est were analysed in an alignment of 34 sequences using the Clustal W tool to discover sequence variations across groups (Gibbs et al., 2015; Thompson et al., 1994). Bioedit 7.2 was used to compute the nucleotide and amino acid sequence compositions, as well as the percent sequence identity (Hall, 1999). Genetic distances (p- distances calcu- lated on nucleotide or amino acid) were calculated using the best- fitted nucleotide substitution model Tamura- Nei
in MEGA version XI.

The software application of DnaSP version 6.10.01 with default settings (Rozas et al., 2017) was used to cal- culate the values of nucleotide diversity (Pi), number of haplotypes (H), haplotype diversity (Hd), number of poly- morphic (segregation) sites (S), the total number of muta- tions (Eta), the average number of nucleotide differences (k), average pairwise nucleotide diversity (p), Tajima's D, Fu and Li's D and F tests for world- B group in which the New Delhi strains grouped into. The neutrality test was conducted based on number of segregating sites and the average number of nucleotide differences of 17 sequences grouped in world- B along with New Delhi strains to access the demographic selection acting on the population. values of nucleotide diversity and Tajima's D were also confirmed through the Tajima's neutrality test in Mega XI. The same software was used to estimate genetic differen- tiation and gene flow between the populations of 36 poly- protein sequences of TuMV isolates categorized based on pathotypes (17 of world- B; 4 of Asian- BR; 8 of basal- BR; 4 of basal- B and 3 of OM- gp) (Table 7) based on the differ- ent permutation statistical tests (KS, KST, Z, Snn and FST) (Hudson, 2000). The three- permutation based statistical tests Ks*, Z and Snn supported by P value less than 0.05 were used. The value of FST varied from 0 to 1 for undiffer- entiated and fully differentiated populations, respectively. If |Fst| < 0.33 or |Nm| = 1, frequent gene flow is considered to have occurrence.
Recombination analyses and selection pressure

The potential recombination events in the 36 TuMV com- plete genome sequences including New Delhi strains were determined using RDP, GENECONV (Sawyer, 1999), BOOTSCAN (Salminen et al., 1995), CHIMEARA (Posada & Crandall, 2001), MAXCHI (Smith, 1992), SISCAN (Gibbs et al., 2000) and 3Seq in conjunction in the RDP version 4.77 software package (Martin et al., 2015). All the isolates that have been recognized as likely recombinants by the RDP version 4 algorithms, using minimum three distinct approaches, were considered and their major and minor parents along with recombination breakpoints were determined.

To determine the kind of selection pressure on the pop- ulation, nonsynonymous (dN) and synonymous (dS) dif- ferences were estimated statistically at individual codon level in the polyprotein by SLAC and FUBAR methods of Data monkey web server (http://www.datam onkey. org/). The site selection pressure data was also confirmed through MEGA 6.0 using Tamura- Nei model (Tamura et al., 2013).

The stunting symptom varied with variety, more promi- nent being in quality mustard (Zero (PM30) and double zero mustard (Pusa double zero mustard 11) as compared to conventional type (Pusa vijay and Pusa Karishma) (Figure 1c). Characterization of putative polyproteins and structure of TuMV genome
Determination of the complete genome sequence of TuMV isolates using RNA- seq approaches

Virome analysis of two mustard samples was done by the ribosomal RNA- depleted RNA- seq approach. In the two libraries, the Illumina sequencing data generated were 123,561,190 and 108,345,808 (150 bp) paired- end reads from black (New Delhi BM) and yellow mustard (New Delhi YM), respectively. After trimming 123,559,805 (av- erage length 134.66 bp) and 108,345,771 (average length 137.11 bp), sequence raw reads were obtained (Table 1). Total number of 37,701 and 51,819 contigs were gener- ated respectively from BM and YM sample of mustard. All contigs were subjected to a BLASTN search against the NCBI nucleotide database, which revealed whole- genome sequences of TuMV. The sequence assembly results ob- tained using de novo assembly and reference- based map- ping were found to be consistent. The reference- based mapping revealed the presence of TuMV in both black and yellow mustard with the number of reads as 1,643,022 (1.33%) and 2,490,504 (2.30%), respectively (Table 1).
Wet- lab validation of TuMV in mustard genotypes

The PCR amplicons of approximately 1065 bp and 86 bp were obtained in all the tested samples for both P3 and CP gene, respectively, whereas negative control showed no amplification during RT- PCR. The amplified sequences were submitted in NCBI and were found to share around 98% sequence similarity with partial cds of CP (AB180011) and around 93% sequence similarity with P3 gene of poly- protein (LC537499). The full- length genome sequences of TuMV strains YM and BM reported in this study were deposited to NCBI with accession numbers: OM469012 and OM469013, re- spectively. The full- length genome sequences were 9817 and 9829 nts (including the 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions [UTR]) ssRNA, respectively. The nucleotide base compo- sition of adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil in the two isolates genomic RNA were not substantially different, with A = 31.84%– 31.90%, C = 20.71%, G = 24.31%– 24.37% and U = 23.08%. In both isolates, the genome contained a single big ORF that translated into 3164- residue poly- protein and was flanked by 5′ UTR of 112 and 124 nt in YM and BM, respectively, and 3′ UTR of 210 nt. The ACAACAU (positions 3– 9; 15– 21, respectively) and UCAAGCA (positions 50– 56; 62– 68, respectively) con- served sequences were found in the 5′- UTR, matching to potyboxes “a” and “b”, which are thought to play a role in transcription initiation.

Nine potential protease cleavage sites were discovered in the polyprotein at amino acid positions 362, 820, 1175, 1227, 1871, 1924, 2116, 2359 and 2876 resulting in 10 mature pro- teins. The P1 and HC- Pro had F/S and G/G cleavage sites, whereas NIa- Pro had Q/V and Q/A, Q/T, Q/N, E/A, E/S, Q/T and Q/A cleavage sites (Table 2). The ORF coding for the putative protein PIPO inside the P3 ORF was identified to be produced by a +1 ribosomal frameshift commencing at a G2A5 motif at position 3058 (Figure 2). This was identical to the G1- 2A6- 7 motif seen in other potyviruses, and it fin- ished with a UAA termination codon at positions 3240- 3243. The genome sequences of BM and YM were 99.8% identical. Since the genome of BM isolate was 12 nts longer in the 5′ UTR, the position of each gene can be calculated by adding 12 nts to the position of same gene determined in YM iso- late. Phylogenetic relationships

The full genome sequences of 37 TuMV isolates, includ- ing the two strains identified in this study, were subjected to phylogenetic analysis to assess the evolutionary connec- tions among the TuMV strains, with potato virus Y refer- ence sequence used as outgroup (Table S1; Figure 3). These TuMV isolates were grouped into five lineages, which corre- sponded to basal- B, basal- BR, Asian- BR, world- B and OMs. The two TuMV strains reported from New Delhi clustered to the world- B group and B3 subgroup. The previously reported CP coding sequence (CDS) of TuMV from Brassica (Arunachal) and Raphanus (Chandigarh) from India, along with that from other coun- tries and ones in this study, were used to study the phylo- genetic lineage (Figure 4a). The multiple sequence comparisons of TuMV CP sequences by log- expectation alignment revealed the presence of conserved motifs in CP sequences of other viruses of this group (Figure 4b).
Percentage identity and genetic distance

According to the pairwise comparisons of the YM and BM genome sequences with that of 34 other TuMV isolates ac- cessible in sequence databases show that the most closely related isolate is CHN212 isolate (LC537499) which was the BR pathotype of world- B3 from China sharing 96.5% nucleotide identity (Table S2). The least nucleotide se- quence identity was 77% shared with the three accessions of the OMs group (AB701690, AB701692 and AB701693). While the nucleotide sequence identity with the respective reference sequence (NC002509) was 95.2%, the nucleotide sequence identity with the previously reported pathotype from yellow mustard was 84.6%. The highest amino acid identity of YM and BM isolates 98% shared with three isolates (LC537499, KC119186, HQ446217) all of China reported from Brassicaceae plants (Figure 3). The least amino acid identity was 86% shared with isolates of the OM group. The amino acid identity with respective refer- ence sequence was 97%. Recombination analysis

Out of 36 genomes, evidence of recombination was re- corded in 21 isolates (58.33%). The two TuMV strains exhibited similar recombination events and were inter- lineage recombinants wherein the isolates Tu- 3 served as major parent and 2J as minor for New Delhi recom- binants. The TuMV strain BM also served as minor parent for isolate GK1 reported from Greece, and it was an inter- lineage recombinant of basal- B and world- B. The majority of recombination sites were found in P3, HC- Pro, 6K1, CI, 6K2, VPg and NIa, which were recombination hotspots in TuMV (Ohshima et al., 2007). Recombination events of all other isolates have not been indicated here (Table 4).
Selection pressure

gene was also checked to determine the evolution, and it was observed that all the genes were under strong negative selections. The highest dN/dS value and in turn selection pressure was for the gene PIPO indicating most of the selec- tion pressure to be imposed on P3 was by PIPO.
Population dynamics

The values of neutrality tests, i.e. Tajima's D, Fu and Li's D and Fu and Li's F tests hypothesize that all the muta- tions are selectively neutral. The Tajima's D value was negative and significantly far away from 0 indicating the action of natural selection on these isolates and low fre- quency of polymorphism. Fu and Li's D*, Fu & Li's F* val- ues for TuMV world- B isolates were negative indicating the affinity to expand with a low degree of polymorphism (Table 6).

The selection pressure operating on the population was determined using polyprotein coding region of 36 TuMV isolates. Most of the codons were found to be under nega- tive (purifying) selection (dN/dS < 1) and few under neutral selection (dN/dS = 1) (Table 5). The codon sites having dN/ dS ratio > 1 in MEGA as well as SLAC and FUBAR were only considered to be under positive (diversifying) selection pressure. The results showed that 14 codon sites at positions (13, 14, 15, 19, 20, 38, 41, 43, 67, 71, 85, 88, 180, 181) were found under positive selection. All the sites under posi- tive selection were found to be in gene P1, indicating P1 to be the most variable gene. All other genes were observed to be under purifying selection in most of these sites sig- nifying selection against most amino acid variations. Each

Furthermore, the number of haplotypes (h) and hap- lotype diversity (Hd) was also estimated for the sequence datasets, which deciphered the total number of haplo- type (h) distribution for the world- B group to be 15 and its haplotype diversity to be 0.978 (Table 6). The number of haplotypes depends on the nucleotide variations. If the sequences of a gene share 100% nucleotide identity, it is considered as a single haplotype. The average pair- wise differences between sequences are calculated using nucleotide diversity. The basal- B group which originated from monocotyledonous Allium plants was estimated to have the greatest nucleotide diversity (supplementary data) while the world- B group had the lowest nucleotide diversity.

Further around 850 years ago in Western Europe, brassica- infecting isolates had diverged into the four lineages of the present worldwide TuMV populations (basal- B, world- B, basal- BR and Asian- BR). About 500 years ago, intercontinental commerce through the ocean had aided the spread of TuMV around the world. DISCUSSION

The TuMV present all around the world causing varied amount of losses was also found in India at high incidence and severity especially in recently famous quality mus- tard varieties. Using sequence data of complete genome as well as from genes encoding 10 viral proteins, a molecular population genetic framework was used to examine the evolution of a highly pathogenic plant RNA virus (TuMV). TuMV emerged around 1000 years ago from a closely related TuMV- like virus (TuMV- OMs) found in wild
TABLE 5 Selection pressure and nucleotide diversity of each coding gene of TuMV isolates (36)

Here, we report the complete genome sequences of two TuMV strains sampled from New Delhi India infect- ing black and yellow mustard. In phylogenetic analysis, the TuMV isolates were grouped into five lineages, cor- responding to basal- B, basal- BR, Asian- BR, world- B and OMs, which were consistent with earlier results (Zhu et al., 2016). In this study, YM and BM genome sequences shared their highest identities with isolates from South- East Asian countries (China, Japan and South Korea) and were clustered in the world- B3 group. The world- B isolates cluster is more variable and widespread and ap- pears to have emerged recently. Based on in vivo and in silico research, it was recently demonstrated that TuMV's “emergence” was most likely a “gene- for- quasi- gene” event (Gibbs et al., 2015). According to it, the phylogenetic clustering of TuMV isolates follows an asymmetric pat- tern known as the XXY pattern. This pattern shows that the amino acids (a.a.) in the OM progenitor ([852V, 1006I] at codon locations 852 and 1006 did not change through- out the divergence, but a.a. in the progenitor in the TuMV other groups did (852K, /852Q/852L; 1006K/1006R). The encoded amino acids shifted from hydrophobic to polar in both sites. The findings of this study were constant with that of Gibbs et al. (2015). At three codon sites (852, 1006, 1548), the two New Delhi strains were all 852Q, 1006R, 1548A, which were conserved in isolates of the world- B group (Figure 3).

et al., 1996). This study reports two new recombinant

strains of TuMV for the first time from India as well as from new hosts. Both were recombinants of world- B3 and Asian- BR isolates which represent the two pathotypes found in South and Southeast Asia. Both parents being from Japan also indicate the possible evolution of TuMV New Delhi strains from the South- East Asian isolates as indicated by phylogenetic tree and genetic distance stud- ies. The strain BM serving as minor parent for basal- B isolate with another basal- B isolate as major parent may conclude the hypothesized theory of evolution of world- B pathotypes shortly after basal- B (Kawakubo et al., 2021). These potential recombination events (PREs) could pos- sibly be considered as adaption events to new hosts and ecological conditions. The phylogenetic and pairwise dis- tance studies suggest the migration of TuMV from South- East Asia to India. Probably the route of entry could be from South- East Asia to South Asia; owing to the maxi- mum sequence identity shared with the isolates from China and Japan at nucleotide and amino acid level as well as recombination studies. While the reverse has been suggested for the other reported Asian- BR isolates from South Asia suggesting migrations from Nepal to Northeast China followed by India, Iran, etc. (Ohshima et al., 2010). The genetic distance studies also indicated the low evolu- tionary distance between the world- B isolates only after the OMs. The genetic distance values between the four pathotypes revealed the world- B pathotype to be least distant with Asian- BR followed by increasing evolution- ary distance in accordance with the phylogenetic lineage. Thus it can be inferred that the world- B and the Asian- BR isolates of TuMV are co- evolving together especially in the Asian countries. Also, the only isolate reported from yellow mustard also belonged to the Asian- BR pathotype reported from Ukraine.

The genetic distance, diversity and variability studies indicated the highly conserved nature of the CP gene fol- lowed by CI gene. While the P1 and P3 were discovered to be most variable and this is consistent with the previ- ous reports (Ohshima et al., 2010). The highly variable nature of P1 protein indicates its possibility in host range determination. The above results were also proved by the

selection pressure studies. This observation is consistent with earlier research (Zhu et al., 2016). The above analy- sis was also noticed when the amino acid sequences of all the genes were aligned by Clustal W in MEGA. Plant virus diversity and adaptability to novel hosts are aided by RNA recombination, which frequently results in the creation of new variations and resistance- breaking viral strains.

The diversifying selection sites were observed only in P1 gene. The positive selections endow the virus with more fitness to adapt to a new host and environment. All other genes were under varying degrees of purifying to neutral selection which attributes in preserving the protein functions and reducing the frequency of less fit virus variants. The highest selection pressure was ob- served in PIPO genes in accordance with the previous studies. As a result, it appears that P3N- PIPO exerted the majority of the selection pressure on P3, which does not explain the occurrence of alternative stop codons in the PIPO ORF (Hillung et al., 2013). This is hypoth- esized to be associated with the function of P3N- PIPO in cell- to- cell movement and overcoming host resis- tance (Choi et al., 2013; Vijayapalani et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2010). The greater selection pressure on P1, P3 and P3N- PIPO might act as a driving factor for host dependency and adaptability (Suehiro et al., 2004;
Vijayapalani et al., 2012).

RNA viruses have such a high mutation rate that a single RNA molecule produces a population of mutant sequences (haplotypes or variations) clustered around a master sequence, termed quasispecies as noticed in the case of TuMV. The negative values in different popula- tion dynamic tests (Tajima's D and Fu and Li's D and F- values) indicated TuMV world- B population tends to- wards a low frequency of polymorphism caused either by background selection, genetic hitchhiking or pop- ulation expansions. Because selection events such as genetic hitchhiking and background selection affect rel- atively small fractions of the genome, a multilocus trend of negative Tajima's D and Fu and Li's D and F- test sta- tistic values indicates that demographic forces are acting on the population (Hey & Harris, 1999; Tajima, 1989). The estimated nucleotide diversity for the isolates of

world- B was found to be significantly low as compared to all other pathotypes. This indicates low genetic diver- sity within the world- B isolates and a fairly stable state of the TuMV world- B population, while the basal- B isolates were found to be the most variable. Based on the statistical tests done, the pathotypes mainly preva- lent in South- Asia and Southeast Asia being world- B3 and Asian- BR were also indicated through the highest amount of gene flow and least genetic differentiation among the isolates proving that they are least distantly related. While the world- B isolates are most distantly re- lated with the OMs. High migration rates favour genetic uniformity between populations decreasing the global genetic diversity (Moya et al., 2004).

Our findings contributed to our understanding of TuMV's evolution, host expansion and genetic conserva- tion in India. The TuMV infection was observed naturally from black mustard for the first time and both the strains from New Delhi were found to be of the world- B3. This also is the first incidence of world- B3 pathotype from South Asian region. The TuMV's pathogenic mechanism and cruciferous crops' resistance to TuMV isolates will be important research topics in the future.
